title: Class 11 Chemistry — Hydrocarbons Study Guide
notes: Acyclic alkanes have formula CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ and C–C single bonds; monoalkenes have CₙH₂ₙ; monoalkynes have CₙH₂ₙ₋₂. Rings or additional unsaturation change these formulae. Alkanes are relatively unreactive; π bonds make alkenes and alkynes undergo addition.

Alkane preparations include haloalkane reduction, Wurtz coupling (two alkyl halides with sodium in dry ether), decarboxylation of sodium carboxylates with soda lime, and catalytic hydrogenation. Alkanes undergo substitution: halogenation under light/heat uses a radical chain; nitration and sulphonation require suitable conditions. Complete combustion gives CO₂ and H₂O; oxygen shortage may produce CO or carbon. Balance equations and state conditions.

Alkenes can be prepared by alcohol dehydration, haloalkane dehydrohalogenation or catalytic hydrogenation of alkynes. Electrophilic addition breaks the π bond. In usual Markovnikov addition of HX, H attaches to the carbon already bearing more H atoms. The peroxide effect is chiefly observed for HBr and gives anti-Markovnikov orientation by a radical pathway; do not generalize it to HCl or HI. Acid-catalyzed hydration produces alcohols; ozonolysis cleaves the double bond to carbonyl products after work-up.

Ethynes can be prepared from calcium carbide and water or by double dehydrohalogenation of suitable dihalides. Alkynes add H₂, HX and water, with selectivity depending on conditions. Terminal alkynes are weakly acidic because H is attached to an sp carbon; they form salts with suitable bases and precipitates with ammoniacal AgNO₃ or cuprous chloride. Internal alkynes lack this terminal H and do not give these tests.

Bromine water and alkaline KMnO₄ (Baeyer's test) are decolorized/reduced by many unsaturated compounds, but these are qualitative indications, not unique structural proof. Similar-size hydrocarbons tend to have higher boiling points as size/surface area rises; branching tends to lower boiling point. Kolbe electrolysis couples carboxylate-derived radicals at the anode; follow the exact conditions and expected product.

keyPoints: Addition occurs at π bonds; substitution replaces an alkane hydrogen.
The peroxide effect is a special HBr radical case, not a general HX rule.
Only terminal alkynes give characteristic ammoniacal Ag⁺/Cu⁺ precipitate tests.
Bromine-water and Baeyer's tests indicate unsaturation but do not identify one specific compound.
Show reagents and conditions above arrows and balance full reactions.
practiceQuestions: Write equations for methane chlorination under light and complete ethane combustion.
Predict the major product of propene + HBr with and without peroxide, explaining the distinction.
Describe a test to distinguish 1-butyne from 2-butyne and explain why it works.
Show one syllabus preparation each for an alkane, alkene and alkyne.
Explain why terminal alkynes are weakly acidic and undergo addition.
summary: Classify the hydrocarbon first, then select reaction patterns appropriate to its bonds. State conditions and remember the limited HBr peroxide effect and terminal-alkyne tests.
